q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the Columbian Exchange after 1492
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE element of the Columbian Exchange described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the catastrophic Native American mortality described in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE long-term effect of the Columbian Exchange on Afro-Eurasia.

sample_answers.a: One element was the transfer of American crops — maize, potatoes, cassava — to the Eastern Hemisphere, where they became staple foods.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the lack of prior exposure: Native populations had been separated from Eurasian disease pools for thousands of years and had no acquired immunity to smallpox, measles, and influenza.
sample_answers.c: One long-term effect was population growth in Europe, Africa, and Asia, as calorie-rich American crops like the potato and maize supported larger populations.

q1.stimulus: The term 'the Columbian Exchange' describes the vast transfer of plants, animals, diseases, and peoples between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492. The exchange was radically unequal in its effects: Old World diseases devastated Native populations that had no immunity, while American crops such as the potato, maize, and cassava later fueled population growth in Europe, Africa, and Asia. No single event reshaped the world's biology more.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Christopher Columbus, letter announcing his first voyage, 1493
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Columbus makes in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage reflects European attitudes toward the Americas in the 1490s.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of Columbus's letter as evidence about the peoples he encountered.

sample_answers.a: He claims to have taken possession of the islands he found on behalf of the Spanish monarchs.
sample_answers.b: The passage reflects the assumption that newly encountered lands could simply be claimed for a European crown and that their inhabitants existed to trade or serve — the legal and mental framework of conquest.
sample_answers.c: Columbus describes the islanders only as trading partners bringing gifts; he records nothing of their societies, languages, or perspectives, and his account was written to secure royal favor and funding for a second voyage.

q2.stimulus: I discovered many islands inhabited by numerous people, and of all of them I took possession for our most fortunate King. They brought us parrots and balls of cotton and spears, and they willingly traded everything they had.

q3.attribution: The Cantino planisphere, Portuguese world map, 1502
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the map that reflects the new geographic knowledge of the early 1500s.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the rapid production of maps like this one after 1492.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the map illustrates the connection between exploration and the Columbian Exchange.

sample_answers.a: The map depicts the eastern coast of South America and the Caribbean as newly known lands, integrated into a world picture that still centers on Europe, Africa, and the Indian Ocean.
sample_answers.b: One cause was state competition: Portugal and Spain raced to chart and claim new coasts, and accurate maps were strategic assets for navigation, trade monopolies, and treaty negotiations such as Tordesillas.
sample_answers.c: The map is itself an instrument of the exchange — charting the Atlantic routes that would carry sugar, silver, enslaved Africans, and diseases between the hemispheres for the next three centuries.

q3.stimulus: The Cantino planisphere, a Portuguese world map of 1502, showing the newly charted coasts of Brazil and the Caribbean alongside Africa, Asia, and the Atlantic Ocean.
